Chapter 4: Medical Evidence and the Case for Design
Let’s take a closer look at the world of medicine and microbiology, but this time, through the lens of design. Imagine for a moment—if nature was originally crafted with purpose and order, then even now, despite everything that’s changed, shouldn’t we still catch glimpses of that design? Studying disease actually gives us a unique window into this question.
Medical research has shown us that so many biological systems are, honestly, just astonishingly complex and beautifully tuned. Take the immune system, for example—it’s not just a single thing. It’s this entire network of cells, signals, and responses, all working together to spot and neutralize threats. Even the simplest bacteria have their own tiny, intricate tools for survival and adaptation. It’s like watching a team where every member has a specific job and plays it perfectly.
Now, when disease shows up, what’s really happening? Most of the time, it’s about something disrupting or hijacking those systems. Pathogens might mimic the body’s own molecules, block important communication signals, or sneak through tiny cracks in our defenses. But here’s what’s fascinating—the fact that these invaders need such clever tricks tells us just how sophisticated our bodies really are. After all, it’s way easier to break a complex machine than to actually build one from the ground up.
When we dig deeper into the medical evidence, we notice that most mutations don’t create brand new features. Instead, they usually degrade what’s already there. Think about sickle cell anemia for a second—it’s often used as an example of a “beneficial mutation.” Yes, it can give some resistance to malaria, but it does that by harming the normal function of red blood cells. So, it’s really a trade-off, not a leap toward something more complex.
As we look at the bigger picture, three patterns start to stand out:
First, irreducible complexity. Many biological systems need all their parts working together, or nothing works at all. That makes it pretty unlikely that they slowly pieced themselves together by accident.
Second, loss of function. Most mutations or adaptations end up removing or tweaking abilities we already had, rather than creating brand new ones.
And third, design in decay. Even when things aren’t working perfectly, you can still see signs that these systems were once designed with purpose and coordination.
All of this points to the idea that life was designed with intention—and that disease is really just a sign that something in that design has been compromised. The evidence doesn’t show us new systems slowly being built from scratch. Instead, it’s about the breakdown and adaptation of systems that were originally whole.
So, what does this mean for medicine? Well, if we try to understand what these biological systems were meant to do in the first place, we can look for ways to help repair or support them, instead of just fighting the symptoms. And honestly, it’s hard not to feel a sense of humility—and wonder—when you realize just how complex and purposeful life is, even when it’s struggling.
